title: Prompt as a Double-Edged Sword: A Dynamic Equilibrium Gradient-Assigned Attack against Graph Prompt Learning

problem.claim: Graph prompt learning is vulnerable to poisoned graph attacks that induce abnormal training through adversarial malicious perturbations.

gap.claim: Existing meta-gradient attacks rely heavily on surrogate GNN training and do not account for GPL settings in which the pretrained GNN is frozen and graph prompt tokens are tuned; their gradient-assigned strategies can also corrupt the topological semantics of influential labeled graphs.

contributions.claim: The authors propose MetaGpro, a dynamic equilibrium gradient-assigned attack against graph prompt learning.
MetaGpro uses surrogate GPL simulation across downstream tasks and integrates over-robust contrastive learning to equilibrate surrogate-model reliability with unstable structures.
The method generates topology perturbations that assign more gradient weight to nodes closer to the misclassification area.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The surrogate GPL outperforms the surrogate GNN in 96% of downstream evaluations.
MetaGpro reduces GPL accuracy by 2%–20% compared with state-of-the-art works in most evaluations.
The authors report that code for MetaGpro is available.

narrative_sequence.summary: GPL bridges graph pretraining models and downstream graph tasks through graph knowledge transfer.
GPL is vulnerable to poisoned graph attacks, while prevalent meta-gradient attacks fail to model the frozen-pretrained-GNN and tuned-prompt-token setting and may damage influential labeled graphs.
MetaGpro combines surrogate GPL simulation, over-robust contrastive learning, and topology-based gradient weighting to improve transferability and mitigate gradient bias.
The authors report stronger surrogate GPL performance than surrogate GNNs in 96% of downstream evaluations and GPL accuracy reductions of 2%–20% against SOTA works mostly.
Code availability for MetaGpro is reported.

source_observation.claim: Attack transferability may benefit from simulating the target learning setup, including frozen pretrained components and tuned prompt tokens.

interpretation.claim: A surrogate that matches the target optimization structure can better represent attack-relevant behavior than a surrogate with a different training configuration.

application.claim: When designing attacks or robustness tests for modular pretrained systems, align surrogate training with the modules and parameters actually optimized downstream.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this alignment is necessary or effective outside the reported GPL downstream evaluations.

source_observation.claim: Excessive perturbations of labeled nodes can create gradient bias, while topology perturbation generation can emphasize nodes near the misclassification area.

interpretation.claim: Controlling perturbation concentration may preserve more reliable surrogate-training signals and focus attack optimization on decision-boundary-relevant regions.

application.claim: In graph attack design, regulate perturbation allocation using structural proximity to likely misclassification regions rather than concentrating changes only on influential labeled graphs.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify how misclassification proximity is measured or whether the approach generalizes to other graph tasks or attack settings.

unknowns: The abstract does not identify the downstream tasks, datasets, baselines, or evaluation protocol.
The abstract does not provide absolute accuracies, attack budgets, perturbation constraints, or statistical uncertainty.
The abstract does not detail the over-robust contrastive learning objective or topology perturbation algorithm.
